See, now You are finally offstage where we can talk. I can’t see through the drapes and pulleys, it’s too dark for me to turn them into moss and oaks, too dark for me to blink wooden risers into a bayou beautiful in near collapse that once ran a monstrous river into the Gulf, a scorched stew powerful only in sufficient stillness. No monstrance, no milagro, no brown scapular scraps, not even a woven palm frond. Just You and me. Just me, actually, standing with hip cocked and three fingers resting on my chin. Not even a naked household goddess above my bed where I ache and ache. I hate the Greeks, those bastards, for figuring You into some kind of flesh—though that cure is just a start. And the Romans tried, but flesh must do more than die: it has to live. And here’s what’s next. Me talking to You in Your most present absence, without even an apophatic clue. I imagine Your holy knees gathered to Your chin and Your arms bound twice around your legs. I imagine Your heart in a corner beating while You listen to my footfalls circle from the best damn hiding place of all.

See, now You are finally offstage, where we might speak. I cannot see through the drapes and pulleys—too dark to conjure moss and oaks from them, too dark to blink these wooden risers into that beautiful, near-collapsing bayou which once carried a monstrous river down to the Gulf, a scorched stew whose power lay only in its stillness. No monstrance here, no milagro, no scraps of brown scapular, not even a woven palm frond. Only You and me. Only me, really—standing with hip cocked, three fingers resting against my chin. And here is what follows: me, speaking to You in Your most present absence, without so much as an apophatic clue to guide me. I picture Your holy knees drawn to Your chin, Your arms wound twice about Your legs. I picture Your heart beating in some corner, listening as my footsteps circle round the finest hiding place there ever was.

---

outputs.L2: Look at this — You've slipped backstage at last, where conversation becomes possible. The curtains and rigging above swallow all light; I lack the vision needed to conjure moss-draped oaks from this darkness, can't will these wooden platforms into that ruined, gorgeous swampland that once channeled a ferocious river toward the Gulf — a charred broth whose only strength lies in absolute quiet. There's no ornate reliquary here, no small miracle-charm, no fragments of blessed cloth, not even a plaited palm leaf. Only the two of us remain. Or rather, only I remain, hip tilted to one side, fingertips pressed against my jaw. Not a single carved deity watches over the bed where my longing never stops. Those Greek philosophers — I despise them — for reducing You to something bodily, though embodiment was merely their opening move. The Romans pushed further, yet a body's purpose can't end in dying; it must also manage to live. So this is where things stand now: I address You within Your overwhelming absence, lacking even the language of negative theology to guide me. I picture Your sacred knees drawn up against Your chin, Your arms wrapped twice around Your folded legs. I picture Your pulse hammering away in some hidden corner as You track the sound of my steps pacing above the finest concealment ever devised.
outputs.L3:
**On the Empty Stage**

You stand before me now in this backstage space, stripped bare of its former magic. Where once the drapes hung heavy with painted shadows, where pulleys once hoisted false moons and risers built the illusion of solid ground beneath uncertain feet—there is nothing now. The moss-covered bayou I conjured for you, that humid dreamscape of cypress and dark water, has been dismantled piece by piece. The ropes lie coiled and useless. The canvas backdrops have been rolled away into storage, into forgetting. What theater is this, that performs only its own absence?

I search for you among what should remain sacred, and find only more emptiness. No monstrance catches the light to hold your radiance in its golden rays. No milagro, no small tin offering shaped like a heart or a leg or a plea, hangs waiting to carry my desperate bargains toward you. The scapular that should rest against my chest, two small cloths bound by faith and string, is nowhere to be found. Even the palm frond, that humble green blessing pressed into hands on a Sunday of ancient triumph, has withered from memory. The household goddess, small and clay-formed, who once watched over hearths and kept vigil through generations—she too has vanished, taking her quiet protection with her.

And so I stand alone. Not merely solitary but achingly, terribly so—the kind of alone that has a texture, a weight, a sound like wind moving through rooms that no longer echo with purpose.

I find myself angry with the Greeks, if I am honest. They took the divine and pressed it into flesh, as if that were enough, as if a body alone could contain what needed containing. They gave gods desires, jealousies, wandering hands and wandering hearts—made them mortal in every way that mattered except the final one. But flesh alone is not revelation. Flesh alone is just another kind of hiding, a costume that fools no one who looks closely enough. Incarnation without consequence is merely theater of a different sort.

The Romans, to their credit, understood something the Greeks did not. They knew that flesh must do more than simply exist—it must die, yes, but more than that: it must *live*, must suffer the full weight of living, must bleed and hunger and weep before it can mean anything at all. They pushed the idea further into its uncomfortable conclusion. Embodiment is not enough; embodiment must be *lived through* to its bitter, transformative end.

So here is what I imagine, standing in this stripped and hollow space: I picture you curled small, fetal, hidden—perhaps behind the last remaining flat of painted scenery, perhaps folded into some crevice of this abandoned stage. I imagine your heart beating there in the dark, small and insistent, a rhythm I cannot see but somehow know. And I circle you, slowly, the way one circles something too fragile or too sacred to touch directly. This backstage—this emptied cathedral of illusion, this place where every prop of faith has been removed—this is the ultimate hiding place. Not because it conceals you from me, but because it is where you have always been most yourself: unstaged, unadorned, curled into the raw center of your own becoming, waiting for flesh to finish what flesh has started.
outputs.L4:
# Backstage with the Hidden God

I have come looking for you again, past the velvet curtains where the stagehands whisper, past the ropes and sandbags suspended like patient guillotines, into this darkness where you apparently prefer to conduct your business. This is not the sanctuary. This is not the nave with its practiced hush, its filtered light through saints rendered in glass. This is backstage, where the machinery of belief creaks and groans, unseen by the congregation who thinks the miracle happens in front of them.

I have brought nothing with me. No monstrance to hold you, that gold sunburst meant to cage radiance in a wafer's small circumference. I left the milagro at home—that tin heart, that tin leg, that small metal prayer shaped like the wound it hopes to heal. I am not wearing my scapular today, that brown cloth promise slung around the neck like a leash for the soul. These are the props of a theater I no longer trust, the costume department of a faith that dresses you in whatever we can bear to look at.

The Greeks tried to give you a body once—chiseled marble, the perfect musculature of Apollo, the studied serenity that suggests divinity is simply humanity perfected, symmetrical, cool to the touch. The Romans copied this, added armor, made you conquerable, made you look like us but better, taller, unbothered by weather or grief. They built temples with your face on them and called it reverence, but it was just another attempt to pin down what refuses pinning, to stop the flood by naming it a river.

I don't want your face. I don't want the version of you that fits in my palm or hangs from a chain or stands in a niche collecting dust and devotion in equal measure. I want you the way you actually are back here, in the dark between the set pieces, where nothing has been arranged for viewing.

And this is what I find: nothing. Which is to say, everything that isn't visible. Which is to say, you.

The absence is not empty. This is the strange grammar of your hiding—that the less I can point to, the more I feel surrounded. It's like a house at night when the specific objects disappear but the whole shape of the room presses closer, more present in its unseen totality than any single lamp-lit chair could be.

I imagine you curled up back here, knees to chest, small the way a child makes themselves small in a game of hide and seek, believing that if they cannot see you, you cannot see them—but wanting, desperately, to be found. Not by everyone. Not by the ones who would drag you into the light and mount you on a wall, who would reduce you to iconography, who would trace your outline in gold leaf and call the tracing holy. But by someone who would sit down in the dark beside you and understand that this—this curled-up hiddenness, this refusal of every image we've built—is the most honest shape you can take.

Maybe this is what I was never taught in catechism: that you do not want to be found the way lost objects are found, restored to their proper place, identified, catalogued. You want to be found the way silence is found in noise—by accident, by patience, by someone willing to stop performing the search and just sit still enough to notice they are not alone.

So I sit here, backstage, in the dark, without my milagro, without my scapular, without the comfortable weight of a monstrance in my hands. I let the Greek marble crumble in my mind. I let the Roman armor rust. I stop asking you to have a face.

And in this absence, I feel you more clearly than I ever did in the nave, more clearly than in any chapel with its careful light. You are curled here beside me, small and hidden and utterly present, teaching me that the deepest intimacy is not seeing you but sitting with you in the not-seeing, that concealment is not your absence but your most vulnerable form of being here.

I do not reach for you. I do not try to coax you into the light where I could describe you to others, where I could make you legible, safe, exhibitable. I simply stay. And staying, I learn that this is what presence has always meant, underneath all our monstrances and milagros and marble gods: not the display, but the darkness that holds us both, unwilling to perform, unwilling to leave.
outputs.L5:
# The Gulf, By the Sea

You stood at the edge of the shore, watching the gulf stretch endlessly before you. The way the sun caught the water's surface made everything shimmer with a golden light that seemed almost impossible to describe.

I remember when you first told me about that place—a quiet stretch of coastline where the gulf meets rolling hills, where you used to spend your summers as a child. You said the water there had a different quality to it, calmer somehow, more forgiving than the open ocean.

"You have to see it to understand," you told me once, and I believed you.

Now, standing here myself, I finally see what you meant. The gulf doesn't crash against the shore the way other seas do. Instead, it seems to breathe in and out, gentle waves lapping at the sand like a slow, steady heartbeat. Fishing boats dot the horizon, their silhouettes small against the vastness of blue that surrounds them.

You always said the sea changes people. Maybe it's the salt air, or the way the horizon stretches beyond what your eyes can hold. Whatever it is, standing here now, I understand why you kept coming back to this particular gulf, year after year, as if searching for something only the water could give you.

Perhaps some places simply become part of who we are. The gulf was yours long before I ever saw it myself—and now, in some small way, it belongs to me too.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem addressed to God as if speaking to an absent figure hiding backstage after a theater performance, blending theatrical imagery with religious doubt.
counterfactuals.output:
**Stage Door**

I know you're back there—
I can see the shadow of your coat
against the exit sign's red glow,
that particular way you hold your breath
when you don't want to be found.

The house lights are up now.
Everyone else has gone home
still holding their playbills,
still asking each other what it meant,
the ending you wrote
and never bothered to explain.

I was good tonight. I hit every mark
you scattered across the stage like breadcrumbs,
said all the lines you gave me
in a language I'm still learning
from a script I've never seen whole—
only these torn pages,
slipped under dressing room doors,
water-stained, half in your hand.

Come out. I won't ask for an encore.
I just want to see your face
without the footlights making it a myth,
without the follow spot turning you
into something too bright to look at directly.

I've stood at this door before.
I know the trick of it—
how you let the silence answer,
how the silence has your voice in it
if I listen long enough,
the way static holds a radio station
just past reaching.

Maybe you're not hiding.
Maybe there's no one back there at all,
just ropes and pulleys,
sandbags counterweighting the empty air,
a greenroom mirror
reflecting only the coat rack,
someone else's discarded costume.

Maybe I've been talking
to the space where a body should be,
the shape a director leaves
blocking scenes for actors
who never learn they're alone up there,
believing every gesture
is a conversation.

Still. I'll knock.
I'll knock the way I always do,
soft enough to seem
like I don't expect an answer,
loud enough
that if you're there,
you'll know I haven't left.

The stage behind me goes dark
one bulb at a time.
I stand in what's left of the light
you might be standing in too,
somewhere just beyond this door,
close enough to hear
if you were listening,
far enough
that I can't be sure
you ever were.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness prose poem about longing for God's presence, using Louisiana bayou and Gulf Coast imagery, Catholic iconography, and classical mythology references.
counterfactuals.output:
**Vespers on the Atchafalaya**

Somewhere between the tupelo gum and the tide, Lord, I am still looking for you—the way the egret looks for stillness in water that will not hold still, the way Orpheus looked back though he knew better, though every myth ever told him don't, and I don't either, I turn my head anyway toward the marsh grass rustling like a rosary dragged through fingers, one bead, one Hail Mary, one dragonfly stitching the heat into something bearable.

The bayou doesn't rush. It broods. It is Purgatorio with cypress knees for kneelers, moss for a mantilla flung over the face of every drowned saint we never canonized, and I am asking you again, the way Persephone must have asked the dark, how long is a season, how long is exile, how long before the pomegranate seeds stop tasting like the only sweetness left in the underworld—

because Gulf water tastes like that. Salt and sugarcane and something underneath, something that could be grace or could be the ghost of grace, the way the incense at St. Martin's holds the shape of prayer after the prayer has gone up and out through the tin roof into a sky the color of Mary's cloak, that impossible blue they paint her in, blue like the hour before hurricane, blue like the hour you were supposed to come and didn't, or did and I was looking at the pelicans instead, diving like something baptized against its will over and over into the same brown water.

Tell me are you the heron standing one-legged in the shallows, patient as Job, patient as the oyster shell working its slow rosary of pain into pearl, tell me are you the crawfish boil steam rising like votives, like the smoke off Vulcan's forge, like every burnt offering Abraham ever almost gave, tell me are you in the fig tree that didn't fruit or the fig tree that did, are you Demeter grieving in every drought that cracks the levee mud into a mosaic of your absence—

I have lit candles for you in gas station Virgins, in dashboard santos swinging like Charon's lantern over black water, I have said your name into the wind off Barataria the way sailors said Poseidon's, half curse, half plea, because what else is prayer but bargaining with a god you can't see who might drown you or might carry you, might be both, might be Christ walking that water and might be nothing but moonlight doing what moonlight does, which is lie beautifully—

and still I want you the way the delta wants the sea, brackish, unresolved, an estuary of a soul mixing sweet water with salt and calling it home, calling it River Jordan, calling it Lethe, calling it whatever you call the place where forgetting and remembering are the same slow current, and I am standing in it up to my knees like John the Baptist, like a boy who lost his mother's ring in the Vermilion and is still, twenty years later, feeling for it in the mud with his bare and stubborn feet,

still feeling, Lord, still feeling for you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental poetry in the voice of someone confronting God directly, incorporating theater/stage metaphors, Catholic religious symbols (monstrance, milagro, scapular), and a critique of how Greeks and Romans depicted divinity in flesh.
counterfactuals.output:
**BLOCKING FOR A GOD WHO WON'T TAKE HIS CUE**

*[lights up on an empty apse]*

You,
upstage of everything,
holding your light like a stagehand
who forgot the show already started —

I've been standing here since Vespers
hitting my mark,
waiting for you to enter
from the wings of the whirlwind.

The Greeks gave you abdomens.
Gave you Apollo's throat, gave you
Zeus in a swan-suit, method-acting
seduction, divinity worn
like a costume that fit
too well — flesh as proof,
marble as scripture,
a god who could be *touched*
because he'd agreed
to be beautiful first.

The Romans just rented the set.
Same gods, new names,
same abs under different togas,
imperial understudies
playing the leads
their conquered towns wrote first.

But you —

you hide.

You go into the wafer
like an actor into a trapdoor,
and call it the whole self,
call the vanishing
*presence.*

*[a monstrance is raised, gold rays like a sunburst backdrop, cheap and holy]*

Is this the blocking, then?
Center stage, encased,
visible only through glass
and gold sunburst spokes,
lit like a marquee
for a show that never opens
to the public —

I keep the milagro in my pocket
like a stub from a performance
I paid for and never saw:
a tin leg for the leg you didn't fix,
a tin heart for the one
still beating wrong,
little scrap-metal reviews
nailed to the set
because the play never resolves,
Act III keeps looping,
the understudy never comes down
from the fly system
to take a single bow.

I wear the scapular
against my sternum
like a placard that says
*I BELONG TO THE PRODUCTION*
even when the production
has canceled its run
and kept selling tickets.

You are the fourth wall
I keep talking through.

You are the god
who would not pose for marble,
would not flex for Athens,
would not let Rome cast you
as a decent-looking emperor —

instead: a smear of wheat
under an artificial sun of gold spikes,
a body so hidden
it isn't a body,
divinity with the stage directions
removed,
so the audience —
me, kneeling, house lights half up —
has to supply the entrance
myself,

has to say *He is here*
into an empty apse
and mean it
like a cue
that never comes,

like a curtain
that is also
the only visible part
of God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that personifies God as a hidden child playing hide-and-seek, using sensuous, embodied language and a mix of religious, mythological, and regional Southern imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Divine Child's Game

He hides in the kudzu's green throat,
giggling behind Spanish moss curtains,
this God-child with dirt-stained knees
who knows every hollow of the pine barrens
better than His own catechism.

I have chased Him through August heat,
that shimmer-veil where the cicadas
scream His hiding place in cicada-tongue,
a Pentecost of insects
betraying nothing, revealing everything.

He smells of magnolia rot and river mud,
of Communion wine spilled on red clay,
this trickster-Christ, this Pan-boy prophet
who leaves His footprints
in the baptismal creek's soft bank
then vanishes like Eurydice—
always just one glance too late.

Grandmother said He hides in the hush
between hymn verses, in the pause
before the preacher's *Amen*,
that God plays hooky from His own omniscience,
tucks Himself behind the hanging Spanish moss
like Zeus disguised as swan, as bull, as rain—
except this time as a boy who bites His lip
to keep from laughing.

I have found His hiding spots before:
once in a mason jar of lightning bugs,
their small combustions like a hundred
burning bushes shrunk to matchbook size;
once in my mother's voice
calling supper through the dusk,
sound made honeysuckle-thick with love;
once in the taste of communion bread
gone stale, gone strange, gone holy
on my tongue like a secret
He wanted me to keep.

But mostly He stays hidden,
this God who plays at Orpheus and hide-and-seek,
who wears the skin of Southern boyhood
sunburnt and grass-stained and eternal,
who calls from the tree line, *Ready or not*—

and I am never ready,
and He is always found
in the almost-seeing,
the glimpse gone quick as swallow-flight,
the holy game that has no ending,
only Him, laughing,
somewhere just behind the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a devotional yet irreverent poem addressing God with intimacy and frustration, exploring absence, embodiment, and the failure of religious symbols to capture divine presence, ending with an image of childlike hiding.
counterfactuals.output:
# Hide and Seek

You again.
Or rather, you *not* again—
same old vacancy dressed up
in incense and stained glass,
same rumor of a face
behind the tabernacle door.

I've lit the candles.
I've said the words that older,
more patient mouths than mine
wore smooth as river stones.
Nothing. Or everything,
which from where I'm kneeling
looks exactly like nothing.

Where were you when the bread
was just bread, when the wine
insisted on being only
what it was—fermented grape,
a Tuesday-evening headache
waiting to happen?

I have loved you the way you love
a scar you're not allowed to touch.
I have shouted into cathedrals
built specifically to swallow shouting.
I have asked and asked
like a child rattling a locked door,
certain someone's laughing
on the other side.

Maybe you don't do burning bushes anymore.
Maybe you got tired of pillars,
tired of being reduced
to weather and coincidence,
to the shape of a face in toast,
to whatever the mystics
could stand to name you.

But I've felt you—
I swear I've felt you—
in the stupid, unbearable ache
of just being a body
in a world that keeps ending
and starting again each morning
like it hasn't noticed the difference.

So here's my last complaint,
lodged with all the others
in whatever inbox
you check on Sabbaths:

If you're going to be silent,
be silent *with* me.
Don't leave. Just
don't answer.

Let me keep looking anyway—
eyes shut, counting slow,
face pressed into my folded arms
against the corner of the couch,
already giggling,
already certain
you're hiding somewhere close,
that this whole ruined world
is just you
holding your breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
